title.en: The Music That Turns Wolves to Women

region.en: Cave of Cruachan, Co. Roscommon, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭羅斯康芒郡克魯阿坎洞

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. VIII, eBook #14465

summary.en: On Samhain night Cascorach the musician spears the fairy woman who comes out of the Cave of Cruachan to take the best of the herds. The deeper affliction is three she-wolves that yearly destroy the sheep — daughters of Airetach of the last people of oppression, robbing in wolf-shape. Only they will come near to men having harps: so Cascorach plays till they stretch themselves to listen, speaks them into their own shapes, and Caoilte's one spear pierces all three — the Valley of the Shapes of the Wolves keeps the name.
summary.zh: 薩溫之夜，樂師卡斯卡拉赫擊殺自克魯阿坎洞出來奪取牛群最佳者之仙女。更深的禍患是每年噬羊的三隻母狼——她們是「最後壓迫者之民」艾雷塔克的三個女兒，以狼形行劫。唯有持豎琴者可近其身：卡斯卡拉赫奏樂使狼俯首傾聽，勸其現出人形，卡爾特一矛貫穿三人——「狼形谷」之名由此而來。

sensitivity.note: The Cave of Cruachan (Oweynagat, 'cave of the cats') is the documented Samhain gate of Connacht, the Irish entrance of the otherworld; the harp-lure-and-shape-reveal is a reverse of the usual enchantment — music unmasking, not bewitching. Coordinates are the real cave.

passages.text: Caoilte was one time at Cruachan of Connacht, and Cascorach was with him, and there he saw sitting on a heap of stones a man with very rough grey hair, steward to the King of Ireland, having a herd of cattle before him in a fenced field. "We have great troubles on us in this district. I have many herds of cattle, and every year at Samhain time, a woman comes out of the hill of the Sidhe of Cruachan and brings away nine of the best out of every herd." "It seems to me that to-night is Samhain night," said Caoilte, and Cascorach went to the door of the hill of the Sidhe, and it was not long till he saw the girl going past him out of the hill of Cruachan, having a beautiful cloak of one colour about her, a gown of yellow silk tied up with a knot between her thighs, two spears in her hands, and she not in dread of anything before her or after her. Then Cascorach blew a blast against her, and put his finger into the thong of his spear, and made a cast at the girl that went through her, and that is the way she was made an end of by Cascorach of the Music.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

passages.text: The steward had a second oppression on him: three she-wolves that come out of the Cave of Cruachan every year and destroy the sheep and the wethers, and go back into the cave again. "They are the three daughters of Airetach, of the last of the people of oppression of the Cave of Cruachan," said Cascorach, "and it is easier for them to do their robbery as wolves than as women. They will only come near to one sort: if they see the world's men having harps for music, they will come near to them." So in the morning he rose up and went to the cairn and stopped on it, playing his harp till the coming of the mists of the evening, and the three wolves came towards him and lay down before him, listening to the music. And Caoilte bade him go to the same place again and say to them it would be better for them to be in the shape of women for listening to music than in the shape of wolves. And they heard that, and they threw off the dark trailing coverings that were about them, for they liked well the sweet music of the Sidhe; and when Caoilte saw them there side by side, elbow by elbow, he made a cast of his spear, and it went through the three women, that they were like a skein of thread drawn together on the spear. And that place got the name of the Valley of the Shapes of the Wolves.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. VIII; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wedding at Ceann Slieve and the Battle with the Men of Dea
title.zh: 克恩斯利夫婚禮與神族之戰

region.en: Ceann Slieve (Slieve Felim), Co. Limerick, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭利默里克郡克恩斯利夫（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. IX, eBook #14465

summary.en: Finn asks the daughter of Conan of Ceann Slieve in marriage and, bound to answer everything, shows his knowledge — of the Dord Fiann sounded by nine men, and of the music that pleased him best: spear-shafts whining in cold wind, cups given out at Almhuin, the gull and the heron, the three sons of Meardha. The Men of Dea take offence that the woman promised to the third best of their champions is taken by a mortal; at the feast Ethne entices Finn out under his hero-bonds, fiery-beaked blackbirds burn the company, and Goll breaks through sixteen battalions to strike down Fionnbhar their king.
summary.zh: 芬恩向克恩斯利夫的科南之女求婚，立誓有問必答，展現其識見——九人合奏的菲亞納號角，以及最悅耳之音：寒風中矛桿的尖嘯、艾倫山宴上遞杯之聲、鷗與鷺的啼鳴。神族震怒：許配給其第三勇者的女子竟被凡人娶走。宴上艾妮以英雄之誓誘芬恩出戶，火喙烏鴉焚燒滿座賓客；戈爾衝破十六營，擊斃其王芬巴爾。

sensitivity.note: The catalogue of Finn's best-loved music is a jewel of Fenian nature-lyric embedded in a wedding-negotiation scene; the hero-bonds (geasa) being used to entrap the hero is the classic geis-trap device. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Finn and the Fianna made a great hunting on the hill of Torc, and it happened that day no one stopped with Finn but only Diorraing. They came to the door of a well-lighted house of the Sidhe on the edge of the wood, belonging to Conan of Ceann Slieve, and got good attendance, and a grand feast was made ready. Finn saw Conan's daughter, Finndealbh, of the Fair Shape, the colour of gold on her curled hair and her eyes as blue as flowers, and he asked her of Conan for his wife. "Leave asking that, Finn, for your own courage is not greater than the courage of the man she is promised to — Fatha, son of the King of Ess Ruadh." "I will get her whether the Men of Dea think good or bad of it," said Finn. Conan put him under bonds as a true hero to answer everything he asked, and Finn gave full answers to them all: who made the Dord Fiann, the Mutterer of the Fianna, made in Ireland by the three sons of Cearmait Honey-Mouth; and what was the music that pleased him best — "the time the seven battalions of the Fianna are gathered in the one place and raise their spear-shafts over their heads, and the sharp whining of the clear cold wind goes through them, that is very sweet to me; and when the drinking-hall is set out in Almhuin and the cup-bearers give out the bright cups, that is very sweet to me; and it is sweet to me to be listening to the voice of the sea-gull and the heron, and the noise of the waves of Traig Liath, the whistle of Lugaidh's Son, and the voice of the cuckoo in the beginning of summer."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

passages.text: But when Finn had answered all the questions so well, Conan said he would give him his daughter, and have a wedding-feast ready at the end of a month. It happened that in the half of the drinking-hall at Almhuin given up to the King of Ireland's son there were sitting two of the Men of Dea, Failbhe Mor and Failbhe Beag, and it is what they said, that it is because they were in that side of the hall it was given up — and Finn going to bring away the woman promised to the third best man of the Tuatha de Danaan, against the will of her father and mother. Fionnbhar, that was king over the Tuatha de Danaan, gathered six good battalions, and later sixteen battalions hidden in a Druid mist came to the lawn before Conan's house; and Ethne, the woman-Druid, said: "Goll will not protect him this time, for I will entice Finn out of the house, however well he is watched." She stood before Finn and put him under the bonds a true hero never broke, to come out to her and run a race; and as they ran, Caoilte, shamed into swiftness, passed the witch and turned and made two equal halves of her. Then the Tuatha de Danaan let out a flock of blackbirds having fiery beaks that burned the people in the house, and Goll rushed out, looking like a tall mountain under his grey shield, and broke through till he reached Fionnbhar their leader, and at the last Fionnbhar of Magh Feabhail fell by the strokes of Goll. There never was a harder battle fought in Ireland, for there was no man on one side or the other had a mind to go back one step before whoever he was fighting against.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. IX; not verbatim.

title.en: The Shadowy One and the Harp of Three Strings
title.zh: 暗影夫人與三弦之豎琴

region.en: Bearnas Mor (Gap of Dunloe), Co. Kerry, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡大山口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. X, eBook #14465

summary.en: A wild pig kills the hounds of the Fianna until Bran masters it, and its screams bring a tall man from the hill who asks its freedom. Inside the Sidhe-house at Glandeirgdeis he strikes the pig with his Druid rod and it becomes a beautiful young woman, Scathach the Shadowy One; Finn asks her in marriage, and her father promises her that very night. But Scathach borrows a harp of iron, bronze and silver — one string sets the hosts of the world crying, one laughing, and the silver string puts them all to sleep — and Finn wakes on Bearnas Mor with no bride.
summary.zh: 一頭野豬殺死菲亞納群犬，直到布蘭將其制服；其尖嘯引出山上高人，求芬恩放生。入仙宅後他以德魯伊杖擊豬，豬化為美貌少女——暗影夫人斯卡薩赫。芬恩求娶，其父允以當夜成婚。然斯卡薩赫借得鐵、銅、銀三弦之豎琴——一弦令舉世痛哭、一弦令舉世大笑、銀弦令舉世沉睡——芬恩醒來時身在山口，新娘無蹤。

sensitivity.note: Scathach here is a Sidhe-bride of the Fenian cycle, distinct from the martial Scathach of Skye who trained Cuchulain — the name-complex is shared between training-island lore and fairy-bride lore; the three-string harp parallels Cormac's branch in its emotional dominion. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: It was on the mountain of Bearnas Mor Finn was hunting, and a great wild pig turned on the hounds of the Fianna and killed the most of them, but Bran made an attack on it then and got the best of it. And the pig began to scream, and with that a very tall man came out of the hill and he asked Finn to let the pig go free. And when he agreed to that, the man brought them into the hill of the Sidhe at Glandeirgdeis; and when they came to the door of the house he struck the pig with his Druid rod, and on the moment it changed into a beautiful young woman, and the name he called her by was Scathach, the Shadowy One.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. X; not verbatim.

passages.text: He made a great feast for the Fianna, and Finn asked the young girl in marriage, and the tall man, her father, said he would give her to him on that very night. But when night came on, Scathach asked the loan of a harp, and it was brought to her. One string it had of iron, and one of bronze, and one of silver. And when the iron string would be played, it would set all the hosts of the world crying and ever crying; and when the bright bronze string would be played, it would set them all laughing from the one day to the same hour on the morrow; and when the silver string would be played, all the men of the whole world would fall into a long sleep. And it is the sleepy silver string the Shadowy One played upon, till Finn and Bran and all his people were in their heavy sleep. And when they awoke at the rising of the sun on the morrow, it is outside on the mountain of Bearnas they were, where they first saw the wild pig.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. X; not verbatim.

title.zh: 戴倫的蜜酒與芬恩的狂亂

region.en: Ford of the Slaine, Co. Leix, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭萊斯郡斯拉因淺灘

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XI, eBook #14465

summary.en: Daireann, daughter of Bodb Dearg, asks Finn for one year as his only wife and half his time after, and when he refuses, offers him a cup of mead — and Finn, under bonds never to refuse anything belonging to a feast, drinks and goes mad, turning on his own people and springing on them every fault he knew. The Fianna walk away in sorrow; thirteen times Caoilte runs after them and brings them back, and by nightfall the bitterness is gone from Finn's tongue and he would sooner have died than lived to remember it.
summary.zh: 波德·迪爾格之女戴倫向芬恩求娶——為其獨妻一年、其後共度半生；被拒後獻上一杯蜜酒。芬恩身負「宴席之物不可拒」之誓，飲之而狂，反目向自己的族人，歷數其所知的一切過失。菲亞納眾人黯然離去；卡爾特十三度追回眾人；夜幕降臨，芬恩恢復神智，寧願自刎也不願活在這段記憶中。

sensitivity.note: The geis-trap again: Finn's taboo of never refusing a feast-gift is weaponised by a Sidhe suitor refused. The madness episode parallels the Ulster war-ríastrad — involuntary transformation under enchantment. Coordinates symbolic at the ford.

passages.text: One time Finn and the Fianna were come to a ford of the Slaine, and they saw on the round rock up over the ford a young woman, having a dress of silk and a green cloak about her, and the golden crown that is the sign of a queen on her head. "I am Daireann, daughter of Bodb Dearg, son of the Dagda, and I am come to be your wife if you will give me the bride-gift I ask — your promise, I to be your only wife through the length of a year, and to have the half of your time after that." "I will not give that promise to any woman of the world, and I will not give it to you."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XI; not verbatim.

passages.text: On that the young woman took a cup of white silver from under a covering, and filled it with strong drink, and gave it to Finn. "It is very strong mead," she said. Now there were bonds on Finn not to refuse anything belonging to a feast, so he took the cup and drank what was in it, and on the moment he was like one gone mad. He turned his face towards the Fianna, and every harm and every fault and every misfortune in battle that he knew against any one of them, he sprang it on them, through the mad drunkenness the young woman had put on him. Then the chief men of the Fianna rose up and left the place, every one setting out for his own country; and Caoilte followed after them: "Fianna of Ireland, do not leave your lord and your leader through the arts and the tricks of a woman of the Sidhe." Thirteen times he went after them, bringing them back to the hill in that way. And with the end of the day and the fall of night the bitterness went from Finn's tongue; and by the time Caoilte had brought back the whole of the Fianna, his sense and his memory were come back to him, and he would sooner have fallen on his sword and got his death, than have stayed living. And that was the hardest day's work Caoilte ever did, unless the day he brought the flock of beasts and birds to Teamhair to ransom Finn from the High King of Ireland.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XI; not verbatim.

title.en: The Red Woman and the Beast with Two Moons

region.zh: 愛爾蘭克里郡王者丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Fenian-Sidhe interface tradition, medieval Irish; Lady Augusta Gregory retelling (1904)

source.work: Lady Augusta Gregory, Gods and Fighting Men (1904), Book IV, ch. XII, eBook #14465

summary.en: A beast like a deer with a boar's head, long horns, and a shining moon on each side runs ahead of a Red Woman who has followed it a month and must follow it till it falls — her life and her three sons' depend on it. Finn defies her, is attacked in the shape of a water-worm and saved by Bran, and all night the hunt follows the bleeding beast into Cnoc-na-righ. Inside the opened hill sits a king of the rainbow-clad musicians; the beast, wooed forth at sunset, dies as Bran masters it — a tall man, says the Red Woman: the King of the Firbolgs, whose people will put great troubles on Ireland after Finn is under the sod.
summary.zh: 野獸如鹿而具豬首長角，兩側各映一輪明月；紅衣女子已追逐它一月，須追至它倒下方能免死——她與三個兒子的性命皆繫於此。芬恩不畏其威，被化為水蟲的她襲擊而賴布蘭得救；整夜追獵血獸至王者丘。開啟的山丘內坐著彩虹衣樂師簇擁的君王；日落時野獸應聲而出，為布蘭所制倒斃——竟是一名高大的男子。紅衣女子道破：此乃弗博爾格之王，其族將於芬恩入土後為害愛爾蘭。

sensitivity.note: The two-mooned beast is a Fenian marvel-beast (marvel-hunt opening a Sidhe-mound is the standard entry device); the dying Firbolg king's prophecy is an eschatological annex linking the Fenian cycle to later history. Symbolic pin.

passages.text: One time the Fianna were in Almhuin, and there came a very misty morning, and Finn said: "Make yourselves ready, and we will go hunting to Gleann-na-Smol." They were not gone far when the mist lifted, and they saw a strange beast coming towards them with the quickness of the wind, and a Red Woman on its track. Narrow feet the beast had, and a head like the head of a boar, and long horns on it; but the rest of it was like a deer, and there was a shining moon on each of its sides. "I do not know its name," said the Red Woman, "though I am on its track since I left the borders of Loch Dearg a month ago, and I never lost sight of it since then; and the two moons that are on its two sides shine through the country all around in the night time. And I must follow it till it falls, or I will lose my own life and the lives of my three sons that are the best fighting men in the whole world."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.

passages.text: "It is little heed I give to yourself or your share of men," said the Red Woman; "and if my three sons were here, they would stand up against you." With that he sounded his horn, and she made a great water-worm of herself and made an attack on Finn, and she would have killed him then and there but for Bran being with him: Bran took a grip of the worm and shook it, and it wound itself round Bran's body, and would have crushed the life out of her, but Finn thrust his sharp sword into its throat. The hunt followed the beast all night, the two moons giving light, and about midnight it began to scatter blood after it, and it never stopped till it went in at the foot of Cnoc-na-righ at the breaking of day. The Red Woman struck the side of the hill with a Druid rod, and a great door opened with sweet music coming from within, and inside there was a king sitting in a golden chair, and his musicians were playing, and no one could know what colour were the dresses of the musicians, for every colour of the rainbow was in them. At sunset Bran made the beast turn and forced it, and its strength flagged and it fell dead — but in place of a beast it was a tall man lying before them. "High King of the Fianna, that is the King of the Firbolgs you have killed; and his people will put great troubles on this country in the time to come, when you yourself, Finn, and your people will be under the sod." And she offered to bring them to the Country of the Young, but Finn answered: "We would not give up our own country if we were to get the whole world as an estate, and the Country of the Young along with it."
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Gregory 1904, Book IV, ch. XII; not verbatim.
